title: A Unified Approach for Computing Wasserstein Barycenters of Discrete and Continuous Measures
claim: Our method's barycenters from mixed discrete and continuous inputs match the exact solution, while the entropic Sinkhorn baseline gives sparse, degraded results.
layout: 2 panels (a)/(b), each a 2x3 grid, inputs and outputs by row
description: The figure has two side-by-side panels, each a 2x3 grid of small square plots. Panel (a) top row shows three input distributions: a pixelated digit 8 on a dark purple background, a solid yellow heart, and a blue scatter of a spiral point cloud. Panel (a) bottom row shows smooth viridis-colored density barycenters computed by FRBary, interpolating the first two inputs on the left, all three in the middle, and the last two on the right. Panel (b) top row shows dense blue point-cloud barycenters from the exact free-support approach, with shapes resembling the (a) bottom row. Panel (b) bottom row shows Sinkhorn free-support barycenters. These are sparse, collapsed arcs and a few stray points. The eye goes first to the colorful density maps and the contrast between the dense and sparse point clouds in (b).
caption: Barycenters from heterogeneous input distributions.
abstract: Computing the unregularized Wasserstein barycenter for measure-valued data is a challenging optimization task. Recent algorithms have been tailored to either discrete measures as point clouds or continuous measures discretized on regular grids. In this work, we propose a primal mirror descent algorithm for computing the exact Wasserstein barycenter in the Fisher-Rao geometry. Our algorithm is a unified approach that is flexible enough to simultaneously cover discrete and absolutely continuous input measures, with convergence guarantees in both settings. In particular, when all input measures are discrete, our algorithm, initialized from any probability density, solves a sequence of semi-discrete optimal transport subproblems and produces absolutely continuous iterates that converge to the discrete barycenter. We use synthetic and real data examples to demonstrate the promising result in terms of accuracy and computational cost.
